items.title: docs: stop publishing performance numbers nobody measured
items.body: Companion cleanup for #196. ## The problem `benchmarks.md` published latency, throughput and resource tables that nobody ever ran: `<5ms` overhead, `p95 35ms`, `700 qps` at four instances, `300` audit writes/sec. They were reasoned from what the architecture *ought* to cost, labelled "target" once at the top of the page — and then quoted in `comparison.md` with the qualifier stripped off, where they read as measured facts about a shipped product. For a project whose pitch is auditability, an invented number is a worse liability than a missing one. The first prospect who measures us discredits the exact attribute we sell. ## What changed **`benchmarks.md`** — 350 lines of fabricated tables → a stub that says plainly nothing is measured, states the one thing we *can* say without measuring (the audit write is synchronous and on the critical path by design, so it can't be optimised out of a benchmark without measuring a gateway we don't ship), explains why we're waiting for a quiet machine rather than publishing shared-VPS numbers, and commits to publishing bad results too. **`comparison.md`** — kept in full; it's the stronger page and needs no benchmarks. Removed only the unmeasured parts (~44 lines touched of 362): | Removed | Replaced with | |---|---| | `<5ms` / `+5ms` overhead, 4 sites | "Not measured", linked to benchmarks.md | | TCO day-estimates + "Break-Even Point: 4-6 months" | A table of what you'd have to rebuild in a custom wrapper — the honest form of that argument | | "Effort Estimate: 1-2 days" | A statement that we have no sample to estimate from | | "Production-optimized", "Battle-tested" | "Not measured", "Typed errors with stable codes" | | PgBouncer `<1ms` vs `+5ms` row | Work-per-query: pool checkout vs authz + SQL guard + synchronous audit write | ## Verification `npm run build` in `website/` passes; all new relative links resolve. The two broken-anchor warnings it reports (`auth-sso#state--persistence`, `roadmap#mysql--mssql-deferred`) are pre-existing in files this PR doesn't touch. Docs only — no code, no behaviour change. ## Not in this PR #196 itself stays open as backlog: the harness gets built when there's a dedicated machine to run it on. Measuring needs no tooling we lack — it needs a box whose p99 means something. Separately, I found a **capability** claim that's wrong independent of any benchmark: README and four doc pages advertise MySQL as a supported query target, but `ConfigFile::validate` rejects `kind: mysql` at boot (`src/config/yaml.rs:351`, `ServerKind::has_adapter`). Out of scope here — filing it separately. Refs #196 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. Autofix is disabled. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Documentation** * Updated benchmark documentation to clarify that performance has not yet been measured. * Added details about request behavior, planned benchmark methodology, and publication criteria. * Removed unsupported performance, time, and cost estimates from comparisons. * Clarified migration effort considerations, per-query gateway behavior, and performance caveats. * Added guidance for measuring deployments and submitting benchmark reports.

items.title: fix: ignore stale updateUrl when current version is latest

labels.name: Bug
labels.description: A error that causes the feature to behave differently than what was expected based on design docs

labels.name: Frontend
labels.description: Frontend development work

items.body:
**Description**:
`organizationVersionStatus` derived status from all entries in `organizationVersionData` — including ones rehydrated from localStorage with no timestamp — while `getOrgsNeedingUpdateOrdered` (which drives `latestVersion` and `updateUrl`) already filtered to only timestamped, session-checked entries. The mismatch meant `versionStatus` could report `updateAvailable` from stale pre-upgrade cache while `latestVersion` returned null (no timestamp), producing the "v available" banner after an Electron auto-update restart.

The fix is to apply the same timestamp guard to `organizationVersionStatus`: only orgs whose data arrived from a live check this session (i.e. `setVersionDataForOrg` was called and recorded a timestamp) produce a status. Cache-only entries continue to populate display data in the Organizations settings tab but can no longer drive the update prompt. With fresh data guaranteed, the `updateAvailable` branch reverts to trusting `data.updateUrl` directly — the backend is authoritative — and the `isNewerVersionAvailable` semver guard (which was compensating for the stale-data problem) is removed.

**Description**:
## Summary

  `CryptoGetAccountBalance` is being throttled out of the steady-state permission
  set. This branch migrates all internal test-client usages away from it, fixes a related regression in the yahcli ivy contract validation scenario.

  ## Changes

  ### `HapiGetAccountBalance` / `QueryVerbs` — deprecate `CryptoGetAccountBalance`

  `HapiGetAccountBalance` no longer submits a `CryptoGetAccountBalance` query.
  It now submits `CryptoGetInfo` and reads the balance from the `AccountInfo`
  response, maintaining the same assertion API for existing callers. All
  `getAccountBalance(...)` factory methods in `QueryVerbs` are marked
  `@Deprecated(forRemoval = true)` and updated to use a fixed node payment,
  directing users to `getAccountDetails` with an authorised payer for new tests.

  `BalanceSnapshot` and `SteadyStateThrottlingTest` are updated accordingly;
  `CryptoGetAccountBalance` is removed from the throttle operation groups in
  the test throttle configuration.

  ### `IvyCryptoScenarioSuite` — stop using `getAccountBalance`

  Replaces `getAccountBalance` with `getAccountInfo` + `accountWith().balance()`
  assertion, and adds explicit `.payingWith(SCENARIO_PAYER_NAME)` to the
  `balanceSnapshot` call.

  ### `HapiGetContractInfo` — fix spurious privileged sub-query

  `assertExpectationsGiven` was unconditionally issuing a
  `getAccountDetails(...).payingWith(GENESIS)` sub-query whenever any expectation
  or registry entry was set — including simple balance checks like
  `.has(contractWith().balance(1))`. This required the GENESIS key (account 0.0.2)
  which yahcli does not have, causing `INVALID_SIGNATURE`. The condition is narrowed
  to only fire when token relationship assertions are actually present
  (`!relationships.isEmpty() || !absentRelationships.isEmpty()`).

  ### `AbstractIvySuite` / `IvyContractScenarioSuite` — explicit scenario payer

  All operations across the shared `ensure*` helpers and `contractScenario` were
  relying on the implicit default payer. Every query and transaction now carries an
  explicit `.payingWith(SCENARIO_PAYER_NAME)`, ensuring only the key yahcli has on
  disk is ever used to sign.

This pull request updates the benchmark results and performance commentary in the `README.md` to reflect the latest measurements and improvements to the ExcelReader library. The changes include updated .NET/runtime versions, revised benchmark numbers, and improved explanations of performance characteristics and tradeoffs, especially for high-cardinality string workloads. The summary and comparison text have also been clarified to better reflect the current state of the library and its competitors.

The most important changes are:

**Benchmark Updates and Results:**
* All benchmark tables and summary statistics have been updated with new timings, memory allocations, and relative performance numbers for ExcelReader and competitor libraries (MiniExcel, Sylvan, SpreadCheetah, Sep, CsvHelper) across XLSX, XLSB, XLS, and CSV formats. This includes both synthetic and real-data workloads, as well as materialized (matched-work) and zero-copy read paths.
* The .NET runtime and SDK versions used for benchmarks have been updated to .NET 10.0.10 (SDK 10.0.302), and references to machine differences and caveats for cross-table comparisons have been removed now that all results are from the same hardware.

**Performance Commentary and Analysis:**
* Commentary has been revised to reflect the new results, including updated speedup and allocation ratios versus competitors, and more accurate descriptions of where ExcelReader leads or matches alternatives.
* The analysis of high-cardinality shared string workloads has been updated: after a fix to the per-reader shared-string deduplication cache (now a pre-sized `string?[]`), ExcelReader allocates less than Sylvan in string-heavy scenarios, where previously it allocated more. ## TL;DR

Adds a landing page for Runway — a single self-contained `website/index.html` in the app's design language — published to GitHub Pages alongside the existing update feed.

- Runway had no website. The GitHub Pages origin at `mstallone.github.io/runway/` served only `appcast.xml` and `pricing_supplement.json` from the `update-feed` branch.
- There was nowhere to point people except the repository README.

## What this changes

- **`website/index.html`** — the whole page: no frameworks, no webfonts, no JavaScript. System font stack, inline SVGs (the repo's real provider marks), and pure-CSS mocks of the product: the dashboard popover with donut and capsule meters, the menu-bar pins pill, the Memory window, and the iOS widgets. Adapts to light/dark via `prefers-color-scheme`; the one animation (meter fills) is gated behind `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- Page order: hero → Menu Bar → Agent Memory → iPhone → Performance (measured table from `docs/performance.md`) → More features → download.
- **`.github/workflows/landing-page.yml`** — publishes `website/` to the `update-feed` branch on merge, mirroring the pricing-supplement workflow: same pinned actions, `keep_files: true`, and the shared `update-feed-publish` concurrency group so it serializes with releases and cannot clobber the appcast.
- **`.github/workflows/deploy-update-feed.yml`** — adds "Publish Landing Page" to the `workflow_run` trigger list (GITHUB_TOKEN pushes don't self-trigger) and mentions the page in the header comment.
- **`README.md`** — one-line website link. **`docs/releasing.md`** — one sentence on how the page ships.
- `website/og.png` (copy of `assets/hero.png`), `app-icon.png`, and `apple-touch-icon.png` are derived from existing repo assets.

- The page hard-codes a few product facts that can drift: the mock's footer says `Runway 0.8.6`, and the performance numbers/"eight more" provider count are point-in-time. All are decorative or linked to `docs/performance.md` for the source of truth.

items.title: fix: Handle close when BlockNodeServiceConnection is interrupted or initialize throws
items.body:
**Description**:
This pull request improves the robustness and correctness of connection management and resource cleanup in the block node streaming implementation. The main changes address proper handling of thread interruption during connection close operations, ensure resources are always released even if initialization fails, and add comprehensive tests to prevent regressions.

**Connection close robustness:**
- Updated `BlockNodeServiceConnection.close()` to drain any pre-existing thread interrupt flag before submitting the close task, and to restore the flag only after cleanup, ensuring the close operation always runs and resources are released even if the thread was interrupted beforehand. [[1]](diffhunk://#diff-da2f1a0d1f027169cf917bdb3f958a3958845555dfa4338738600ceee6fa02d2R199) [[2]](diffhunk://#diff-da2f1a0d1f027169cf917bdb3f958a3958845555dfa4338738600ceee6fa02d2L208-R209) [[3]](diffhunk://#diff-da2f1a0d1f027169cf917bdb3f958a3958845555dfa4338738600ceee6fa02d2R218-R220)

**Resource cleanup guarantees:**
- Moved the call to `svcConnection.initialize()` inside the try block in `RetrieveBlockNodeStatusTask.call()` so that `close()` is always called, even if initialization throws, preventing resource leaks.

**Testing improvements:**
- Added a unit test to verify that `close()` is called if `initialize()` fails in `RetrieveBlockNodeStatusTask`, ensuring proper cleanup on initialization errors.
- Added a deterministic test to verify that `close()` completes and the client is properly closed even if the thread's interrupt flag is set before calling `close()`, preventing regressions on interrupt handling.

## Summary
This PR rebuilds the quantitative trading pipeline from scratch with actual, working implementations of all previously-missing modules. The repo previously claimed specific backtest results but had no `src/` code to produce them — only orphaned state files. This commit implements the complete pipeline (data loading, feature engineering, ML models, risk sizing, paper trading, backtesting, reporting) alongside a comprehensive investing terminology glossary to support learning.

## Key Changes

**Core Pipeline Implementation**
- `src/data/weekly_loader.py`: Daily OHLCV download via yfinance and resampling to Friday-ending weekly candles
- `src/features/seasonal_features.py`: Technical indicators (SMA, RSI, momentum, volatility) and seasonal encodings without external `ta` dependency
- `src/features/macro_features.py`: VIX, 10-Year Treasury yield, and US Dollar Index integration
- `src/models/weekly_model.py`: Directional classifier ensemble (RandomForest, HistGradientBoosting, XGBoost fallback)
- `src/paper_trading/risk_engine.py`: Volatility-targeted risk-parity position sizing with confidence thresholding
- `src/paper_trading/portfolio.py`: Simulated portfolio manager with persistent state and append-only trade history
- `src/backtest/walkforward.py`: Out-of-sample walk-forward backtester with expanding training windows
- `src/analytics/quant_metrics.py`: Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, max drawdown, and win rate calculations
- `src/evaluator/seasonal_evaluator.py`: Year-over-Year pattern comparison and recent-weeks summaries
- `src/reports/report_generator.py`: Markdown report generation with embedded glossary links

**Research & Learning Infrastructure**
- `glossary/`: 30+ plain-English explanations of investing and quant terms (Sharpe ratio, risk parity, VIX, etc.) with worked examples and cross-links
- `glossary/INDEX.md`: Browsable index organized by category (Market Structure, Fundamentals, Technical Analysis, Macro, Risk & Portfolio, Quant/ML, Psychology)
- `research_log/`: Predictions log CSV (auto-appended by runner) and entry templates for post-run analysis
- `research_log/entries/EXAMPLE.md`: Filled-in example showing how to close the loop between prediction and outcome

**Testing & Synthetic Data**
- `tests/synthetic_data.py`: OHLCV generators for unit tests (no network dependency)
- `tests/test_weekly_pipeline.py`: Tests for resampling, feature generation, and model training
- `tests/test_quant_enhancements.py`: Tests for risk metrics, risk engine, portfolio, and end-to-end pipeline

**Documentation & Configuration**
- `PLAN.md`: Detailed roadmap explaining the two-track learning system (quant practice + investing literacy)
- Updated `README.md`: Clarifies the rebuild, removes unverified performance claims, explains the glossary-linked reporting system
- `.gitignore`: Excludes generated reports and Python artifacts

## Description

The README published performance numbers that no test produced. Measuring them found the headline claim was not merely unverified but backwards.

**Round trips** — now counted at the `KVStorage` seam and enforced on every CI run:

| Claim in docs | Measured |
|---|---|
| V2 `Find()` "3 RTT (fixed)" | **1** — `fetchTrieData` pipelines both `HGetAll` calls, and a pipeline is one trip. The docs understated ACOR by 3x. |
| V1 `Find()` "O(N×3-5) RTT" | **1**, at any dictionary size. The claim was false. |
| V1 `Add()` "O(M×3-10) RTT" | Shape correct, constant larger — 53 RTT at 5 chars, 507 at 26 |
| V2 `Add()` "2-3 RTT" | **2**, flat ✅ |

**Timings** against a real server (Apple M4, Redis 8, 1000 keywords):

- uncached V2 `Find()` is **~9x slower** than V1, not "50-60x faster". It rebuilds the match engine per call (1.26 MB, 11,704 allocs/op) while V1 memoizes its engine after a single `SMEMBERS`.
- the real speedups belong to `EnableCache` (~15x) and `Preset` (~58x), not to the schema
- V2's unambiguous win is `Add()`, at ~12x

### Design

Two kinds of evidence, deliberately not interchangeable:

- **Structural (round trips)** — counted above the wire, so miniredis and a real server report identical numbers. A test asserts exactly that. CI-enforced, cannot flake.
- **Timing** — hardware-bound. Published with full provenance and stated as *ratios*; repeat runs moved absolute numbers 20-25% while ratios held within 15%.

Pipelines count as one trip, not one per queued command — guarded by its own test, since getting it wrong would inflate every number in the direction that flatters us.

Timing benchmarks now require a real server. Every pre-existing benchmark ran on miniredis, where a round trip is nearly free — precisely where V1 loses, so miniredis understated V2 while appearing to measure it.

**No production code changed.**

## Type of Change

- [x] Documentation update
- [x] Test update

## Checklist

- [x] Tests pass (`make test`)
- [x] Vet/`make vet`
- [x] Linting passes (`make lint`)

## Additional Notes

New docs page: `docs/content/reference/benchmarks.md` — reproduce command (~20s), provenance, run-to-run variance, and the numbers where ACOR *loses*.

CI gains two steps on the existing integration job: RTT verification against both redis and valkey, and a `-benchtime=1x` smoke so the published benchmarks cannot rot. Neither gates on a duration.

items.title: Milestone 6: add provenance-pinned external baselines
items.body:
## Objective

Add the first real external/state-of-the-art comparison track without weakening the repository's reproducibility contract or vendoring arbitrary third-party source into the core.

This milestone turns two previously documented research families into executable, provenance-pinned baselines:

- `orlp/pdqsort` at `b1ef26a55cdb60d236a5cb199c4234c704f46726` (zlib)
- `ips4o/ips4o` at `08a5b926ee65cef19139057c6bde02bb5542c1cb` (BSD-2-Clause)

## External provenance contract

Adds `external/baselines.json` with full upstream repository, exact 40-character commit, declared license, license path, required source paths, include root, and adapter identity.

Adds `tools/bootstrap_external.py`:

- no hidden CMake downloads;
- clone/fetch exact pinned commit only;
- detached checkout at the pinned SHA;
- reject wrong-commit checkouts;
- reject dirty external source trees;
- verify all required paths;
- `--check` mode performs verification without network access;
- self-test uses a real temporary Git repository and confirms dirty-tree rejection.

Adds `tools/verify_external.py` to emit machine-readable provenance containing the upstream commit, Git tree SHA, license identity, and SHA-256 of the actual license file used by the materialized checkout.

`external/vendor/` is ignored so third-party code is never accidentally incorporated into the repository's own source history.

## Paired external benchmark

Adds the opt-in `sort_external` executable.

Algorithms in the first track:

- `pdqsort`
- `pdqsort_branchless`
- `ips4o_sequential`
- sortlab `intro`
- sortlab `quick_3way`
- sortlab `radix_lsd_11`
- `std_sort`

All seven algorithms/controls receive the **same deterministic input within a trial** and execute in a deterministic randomized order using the existing workload/seed/fingerprint contract.

Every CSV row carries:

- algorithm;
- origin;
- pinned upstream commit;
- declared license;
- pattern/size/trial identity;
- experiment/trial seed;
- input fingerprint;
- execution order;
- elapsed nanoseconds;
- correctness verification.

The adapter does not fabricate comparisons, swaps, writes, allocations, or hardware behavior that the external interfaces do not expose.

## IPS4o scope

Only sequential `ips4o::sort` is used. The parallel API is intentionally excluded from this track because thread count, affinity, NUMA topology, scheduler behavior, and scaling change the experiment model.

The pinned official IPS4o tree was inspected directly. Although its README retains recursive-clone wording, `.gitmodules` is empty at this commit and the required include tree is committed in the pinned tree.

The external adapter uses the same compilation flags as its internal controls instead of allowing an upstream CMake project to add a private `-march=native` advantage only to one competitor.

## Opt-in CMake integration

Adds `SORTLAB_ENABLE_EXTERNAL_BASELINES=OFF` by default.

When enabled, configuration fails closed unless the exact required external files are present under the materialized pinned checkouts. CMake itself performs no network access.

```sh
python3 tools/bootstrap_external.py
python3 tools/verify_external.py --output external/provenance.json
cmake -S . -B build-external -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DSORTLAB_ENABLE_EXTERNAL_BASELINES=ON
cmake --build build-external -j
ctest --test-dir build-external --output-on-failure
```

## Tier-2 external campaign

Adds `campaigns/external-v1.json` with two controlled repetitions, 51 independent trials, all 15 workload families, a dense size grid from 16 through 1,048,576, paired `std_sort` analysis, bootstrap uncertainty, and crossover detection.

Two external-track hypotheses are preregistered in `docs/external-baselines.md`:

- **E1:** engineered/pattern-defeating and branchless quicksort can change the quicksort frontier in scoped domains, but no universal dominance is assumed;
- **E2:** sequential IPS4o may have a machine/workload-dependent large-n crossover, which must be estimated rather than asserted as one constant.

Both begin untested. No external performance numbers are promoted by this PR.

## Documentation

Adds or updates:

- `external/README.md`
- `docs/external-baselines.md`
- `docs/algorithm-catalog.md`
- `campaigns/README.md`
- project/CITATION version `0.6.0`

The algorithm catalog now distinguishes implemented external baselines from still-separate future tracks such as VQSort, BlockQuicksort, QuickXsort/QuickMergesort, sorting networks, parallel sorting, NUMA, and external-memory sorting.

## Validation

Local validation before publication:

```text
bootstrap_external.py real temporary-git self-test     PASS
Python bytecode compilation                            PASS
baselines.json parse                                   PASS
external-v1.json parse                                 PASS
sort_external strict C++23 warning build with stubs    PASS
  -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wconversion -Wshadow
sort_external deterministic correctness self-test      PASS
CMake external option configure/build                  PASS
CTest external_sort_self_test                          PASS
```

The pinned upstream APIs were also inspected at their exact commits to verify `pdqsort`, `pdqsort_branchless`, and `ips4o::sort` are the intended interfaces.

Hosted GitHub Actions are not required for this milestone; validation is local and CTest-wired.

items.title: fix: preserve signed transaction body bytes on re-serialization
items.body:
**Description**:

Stop `_BuildTransaction` from re-marshalling an unchanged transaction body. It unmarshalled `SignedTransaction.BodyBytes`, re-applied the same field values, and always re-marshalled — but protobuf serialization is not guaranteed to be byte-for-byte deterministic across implementations/versions, so a semantically-identical body could serialize to different bytes. Any signature computed over the original bytes (e.g. produced by another SDK or another signer in a multi-party flow) then failed to validate.

* Apply the body updates to a `protobuf.Clone` of the decoded body and re-serialize only when `protobuf.Equal` reports an actual change, reusing the original bytes verbatim otherwise
* Rebuild `MaxCustomFees` instead of appending to it so re-building an already-populated body stays idempotent (the old append doubled the list on every serialization)
* Add unit tests covering signed body-byte preservation across a deserialize/serialize round-trip (single- and multi-party signatures over non-canonical bytes) and no custom-fee-limit duplication on re-serialization

**Related issue(s)**:

Fixes #1436

items.body:
## What

Adds RFC 0009: move the invariant machinery the compiler currently duplicates into every generated component (flush pipeline, dirty tracking, host update scopes, effect cleanup, event abort management, prop/attribute plumbing, keyed-list reconciliation, style adoption, registration) into `@naos-ui/runtime` as tree-shakeable free functions over a per-instance kernel record — explicitly **not** a base class.

Motivation is measured, not assumed: current output is 5–17× the authored TSX, and 3.3 KB per module (26 methods) is byte-identical across all 16 example components — up to 52 % of a small component. A feature-equivalent A/B prototype comparison (base class vs. functional kernel) showed equal performance and memory, but the functional variant bundles 37 % smaller for static components because a base class is atomic for tree-shaking.

The RFC includes:

* the kernel design and the generated-shell shape the compiler would emit
* packaging/versioning (`@naos-ui/runtime/internal` as compiler-output contract, `--standalone` inlining flag as escape hatch)
* a six-phase incremental migration plan for codegen
* required revisions to ADR 0013 and `docs/runtime-boundary.md`
* the full measurement appendix

Also adds the RFC to the index in `docs/rfcs/README.md`.

Docs-only change (two Markdown files); no code paths affected. Markdown is outside the `format:check` glob (`**/*.{ts,tsx,mts,js,mjs,cjs}`), so no formatting gate applies. items.title: fix(frigate): modernize GPU compute runtime so device: GPU works
items.body:
Fixes OpenVINO GPU detection on Panther Lake. The base `-vaapi` image bundles a
GPU compute runtime from Jan 2025 GitHub debs (level-zero-gpu 1.6, IGC 2.5.6,
opencl-icd 24.52) that predates support for the newer xe/Panther Lake host
driver, so `detectors.openvino.device: GPU` fails to load even though the NPU
works. This rebuilds the compute runtime with the identical modern kobuk-PPA set
the host already runs and adds the device passthrough GPU compute needs.

What changed
- `docker/main/Dockerfile.vaapi` purges the stale GPU runtime packages and
  installs the modern kobuk-PPA set (`intel-opencl-icd` 26.22.38646,
  `libze-intel-gpu1`, `libze1` 1.28.6, `libigc2` 2.36.5, `libigdgmm12`) so
  OpenVINO can enumerate and compile for `device: GPU`.
- `compose/docker-compose.yml` passes `/dev/dri/card0` alongside `renderD128`
  and `/dev/accel` (GPU compute needs card0 + renderD128; VAAPI needs only
  renderD128).
- `scripts/verify-gpu.py` added, baked in as `verify-frigate-gpu` by
  `build.sh`, mirroring `verify-frigate-npu` for a definitive on-GPU check.
- README updated with GPU detection setup, the GPU verify check, and the
  validated performance/power numbers.

Validation
- `bash -n build.sh`, Python compile of the new script, and YAML all clean.
- Matches the derived image validated live on an MS-03: Level Zero enumerates
  the iGPU, OpenVINO reports `['CPU','GPU','NPU']`, the model compiles to GPU,
  and a 4-camera YOLOv9-tiny workload runs ~8ms/inference at ~80-90 FPS.
- NPU and GPU tie on speed; NPU draws ~11W less at the wall, so NPU stays the
  recommended default for always-on hosts.

items.title: feat(harness): E2-S4 adapter conformance suite
items.body:
Per the sequencing decision for E2: the conformance suite is written first, against fakes, as the executable adapter contract -- before any real SDK (WebLLM/Transformers.js/wllama) is touched. The goal is that the "uniform interface" promise in 03-architecture.md's C3 gets one definition, checked mechanically, instead of getting quietly renegotiated three times to fit whatever each library happens to do.

Extends CellAdapter (E1-S2) with a required `meta` field (runtime/runtimeVersion/supportsWorker) -- the one piece of the full C3 RuntimeAdapter shape (init/generate/embed/dispose/meta) that belongs on the adapter itself rather than being supplied separately by a caller, since only the adapter genuinely knows which exact pinned library version produced a result. Updated the one fakeAdapter() factory in runner.test.ts (everything else spreads from it) and all 90 existing E1 tests still pass unchanged.

Adds packages/harness/src/adapterConformance.ts: five check functions (checkAdapterMeta, checkInitAndDispose, checkRunOnceLifecycle, checkMidRunDisposeAborts, checkErrorSurfacing) -- plain async functions that throw descriptively on failure, meant to be wrapped in individual it() blocks by each real adapter's own test file for granular pass/fail reporting. checkMidRunDisposeAborts in particular verifies an in-flight runOnce() settles promptly when dispose() is called concurrently, since that's what the Stop button (06-security-privacy.md §6.4) depends on.

18 new tests in adapterConformance.test.ts prove the suite has teeth: a well-behaved fake passes every check, and a battery of deliberately broken fakes (empty meta.runtime, negative ttftMs, non-integer tokensGenerated, hanging runOnce()+dispose(), non-Error rejection, empty-message Error) each get caught by name. 108 tests total across the harness package.

Adds packages/harness/src/adapters/{README.md,QUIRKS.md}: the E2 test boundary decision (contract tests in Node/CI now; WASM-path Playwright smoke per adapter in CI; WebGPU-path correctness-only via SwiftShader in CI, per 08-delivery-plan.md §6.4; real performance numbers via the device-lab protocol, never CI) written down once before S1/S2/S3 rather than re-litigated per adapter; the version-pinning reminder from ADR 5.4 (exact versions once real adapters land, not the loose spike-era ranges currently in apps/web); and an empty QUIRKS.md ready for E2-S1 to start filling in.

items.title: feat: reproducible scale benchmark generator
items.body:
Pre-release block, item 3 (the last technical one).

## What

`examples/gen_scale_log.rs`: generates the synthetic Delta logs behind the README's performance numbers, so anyone can reproduce them. Three shapes, from least to most production-like:

1. one JSON commit with N adds (what the old numbers measured)
2. the same files across N commits (listing and replay overhead)
3. N commits consolidated by a **real kernel-written parquet checkpoint** (`Snapshot::checkpoint`; it requires the multi-threaded executor — the builder's default deadlocks, documented in a comment)

## The numbers (200k files, re-measured)

| Shape | Baseline | Predicate | Peak RAM |
|---|---|---|---|
| single commit | ~1.0 s | ~1.3 s | ~280 MB |
| 2000 commits | ~1.4 s | ~2.2 s | ~320 MB |
| 2000 commits + checkpoint | ~0.8 s | ~1.0 s | ~240 MB |

The headline closes the scale question honestly and favorably: **the most production-like shape is also the fastest** — one parquet checkpoint reads better than thousands of loose JSON commits. README's Performance notes and docs/validation.md updated with the table and the reproduction command; the "pending benchmark tooling" caveat is gone because the tooling now exists.
